CausalChain: Chronic HBV/HCV infection -> dysregulated m6A regulators (elevated METTL3, imbalanced FTO) -> aberrant m6A modification on viral and host mRNAs -> destabilization of tumor suppressor and antiviral transcripts (via YTHDF2-mediated decay) -> impaired immune surveillance and enhanced viral persistence -> creation of an immune-tolerant, pro-oncogenic microenvironment -> liver carcinogenesis
Hypothesis: In hepatocellular carcinoma, especially in HBV/HCV-associated cases, dysregulated m6A machinery simultaneously destabilizes host tumor suppressor mRNAs and modifies viral transcripts, thereby undermining antiviral immunity and fostering an immune-tolerant microenvironment that promotes oncogenesis. Targeted correction of these m6A marks could restore mRNA homeostasis and immune function, providing a novel therapeutic avenue.
Abstract: Recent evidence suggests that dysregulation of m6A RNA modification plays a pivotal role in liver carcinogenesis. We propose that in the context of chronic HBV/HCV infections, altered activities of m6A regulators—specifically an overactive METTL3 and unbalanced FTO—simultaneously perturb the stability and translation of host tumor suppressor transcripts as well as viral RNAs. This dual modulation can impair host antiviral responses and disturb immune surveillance by promoting rapid degradation of critical mRNAs that would otherwise counteract oncogenic processes. Our hypothesis implies that precise m6A editing in both host and viral RNAs might restore proper immune function and cellular homeostasis, representing a novel therapeutic strategy to counteract HCC progression.
